mainEntity.name: Is toothache at night a dental emergency?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not all night-time toothache constitutes a dental emergency, but certain symptoms should prompt you to seek urgent care. If your pain is severe and unmanageable, is accompanied by facial swelling, fever, or difficulty swallowing or breathing, you should seek emergency dental or medical assessment promptly. Moderate, persistent toothache that has lasted more than a couple of days should be assessed by a dentist at the earliest available opportunity. Most dental practices offer emergency appointments, and it is always better to have the issue evaluated sooner rather than waiting to see if it resolves.

mainEntity.name: Can a toothache go away on its own?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, mild toothache caused by temporary sensitivity — for example, following a new filling settling in — may resolve without intervention. However, toothache caused by decay, infection, a cracked tooth, or gum disease is unlikely to resolve without professional treatment. Even if the pain diminishes temporarily, the underlying cause typically remains and may progress. Dental abscesses, in particular, can sometimes appear to "settle" while actually continuing to cause damage beneath the surface. Professional assessment is always advisable when toothache persists.

mainEntity.name: Why does lying down make toothache worse?

acceptedAnswer.text: When you lie down, blood circulation to the head and face increases because gravity no longer draws blood toward the lower body. This elevated blood pressure in the region surrounding an inflamed or infected tooth can intensify the throbbing sensation. In addition, lying down changes how the jaw rests and may place subtle pressure on sensitive areas. The absence of daytime distractions also means the brain has little to focus on other than the pain signal, making the experience feel more intense even if the clinical severity has not changed.

mainEntity.name: Could stress be causing my night-time toothache?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stress can contribute indirectly to night-time dental pain in several ways. It is a significant driver of bruxism (tooth grinding), which places considerable force on teeth and can cause cracks, worn enamel, and jaw muscle pain. Stress may also lead to neglect of oral hygiene routines, altered diet, and reduced saliva production — all of which can increase the risk of dental problems. If you suspect stress is affecting your dental health, your dentist can assess for signs of grinding and discuss appropriate strategies, which may include a custom occlusal splint to protect your teeth during sleep.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if I have toothache but cannot see a dentist immediately?

acceptedAnswer.text: While waiting for a dental appointment, you may be able to manage discomfort using over-the-counter pain relief such as ibuprofen or paracetamol, following the instructions on the packaging and considering any personal medical circumstances. Keeping your head slightly elevated when resting, avoiding very hot or cold foods, and rinsing gently with warm salted water may also provide some temporary relief. Clove oil applied sparingly to the affected tooth is a traditional short-term remedy. None of these measures treat the underlying cause, and a dental appointment should be sought as soon as possible.

mainEntity.name: How can I prevent toothache from recurring?

acceptedAnswer.text: Preventing toothache centres on consistent oral hygiene and regular professional care. Brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between teeth with floss or interdental brushes, moderating sugar and acidic food intake, and attending regular dental check-ups all contribute significantly to reducing the risk of decay and gum disease — the most common causes of toothache. If you grind your teeth, discussing this with your dentist may help protect your teeth from the mechanical damage that can lead to pain. A personalised prevention plan developed with your dental team is the most effective approach.
